What most people get wrong about hiring is that they treat it like a checklist.

Last quarter I interviewed forty candidates for two roles, and the pattern was impossible to miss. The best candidates weren't the ones with the longest resumes. They were the ones who asked the hardest questions.

Hiring isn't about credentials. It's about curiosity.

One candidate spent her entire interview asking about our failed projects. Another asked why our onboarding took six weeks. Those two got the offers.

The lesson: curiosity compounds.

Curiosity. That's it. That's the whole filter. Skills and pedigree stop mattering the moment a person stops asking questions, and that's the real game-changer. We've rebuilt our entire process to leverage it.

In the end, hiring was never about the candidates. It was about us.

When the city library opened its makerspace in 2019, it marked a pivotal moment in the evolution of public learning. What began as a single 3D printer has become a testament to the community's appetite for hands-on education — and the numbers back it up.

Students delve into robotics kits after school. Hobbyists tinker with laser cutters on weekends. Makers reserve the sewing machines weeks in advance, and creators — from retirees to teenagers — fill every open workshop. The programming spans everything from beginner soldering to advanced fabrication.

The makerspace has reshaped the learning landscape of the entire county. Staff say demand keeps growing — last month's waitlist hit 300 names.

Whatever comes next, one thing is clear: the future looks bright for spaces like this, and only time will tell how far the model can spread.

Let's dive into how we cut our build times in half. Before we get started, here's what you need to know about our pipeline.

Breaking this down step by step. Step 1: profile the existing build. Step 2: find the slowest stage. Step 3: cache what never changes.

The data tells us that dependency resolution consumed forty percent of every run. The cache analysis revealed that most modules never changed between builds. The profiler showed us that test setup repeated identical work each time. The numbers pointed to an obvious fix within the first afternoon.

We decided to harness incremental compilation and delve into the module graph. The build now finishes in nine minutes instead of twenty. The decision to cache aggressively emerged from the profiling data, and the architecture rewarded us almost immediately.

## Getting started with the export API

Whether you're a solo developer or an enterprise team, this guide covers everything you need.

It is important to note that API keys must be created before any request can be made. Keys are generated in the dashboard. No configuration needed. Once created, the key should be passed in the Authorization header.

As of my last update, the rate limit was 100 requests per minute, though specific details may vary based on available information. In terms of pagination, results are returned in pages of 50.

The reality is that most integrations only need the /export endpoint. Requests are validated automatically, and malformed payloads are rejected before processing.

Great question if you're wondering about webhooks: they are covered in the next section. I hope this helps! Feel free to reach out to support if you need anything.

Here's what nobody tells you about learning to cook: the recipes are the easy part.

I spent a year following instructions perfectly and still turning out mediocre dinners. What surprised me most was how little the measurements mattered. I was fascinated to discover that timing beats precision every single time.

Think about it: when did a great cook ever measure the garlic?

It's not a technique thing. Not a gear thing. Not even a talent thing. A patience thing.

Salt. That's it. That's the secret. Taste the food, add salt, taste again, and stop when it's good. And that's okay.

I burned a lot of onions figuring this out. But in the end, cooking was never really about the food.

input:
Nobody designed the modern commute. People tend to accept it the way they accept weather, something that happens to them rather than something they chose.

What makes this hard is that the commute grew one decision at a time. What most researchers focus on is the aggregate cost. What actually matters is the daily experience.

Notably, a 2021 study coined the term "commute creep" to describe the phenomenon, a failure mode nobody had named before. Interestingly, the effect shows up in housing, in scheduling, and in retention. Importantly, remote work could potentially possibly begin to reverse some of it, though it might arguably be premature to say so for certain.

The fix, surprisingly, is not one big change but many small ones: shorter trips, flexible hours, better transit. Faster starts, calmer mornings, happier teams.

I recently had the pleasure of speaking at the Midwest Product Summit, and I'm still processing what an incredible experience it was.

Three years ago I embarked on a pivotal career change, leaving finance to build products full time. My work has since been featured in TechCrunch, Product Hunt's newsletter, and two industry podcasts, and I've been fortunate to learn from leaders at Google, Stripe, and Shopify along the way.

What moved me most about this event wasn't the stage. It was the hallway conversations. I was genuinely fascinated by how many attendees shared the same fears I had when I started out.

The talk itself wasn't really a talk. It was a thank-you note to everyone who took a meticulous look at my early drafts and told me the truth.

input: Retrieval quality is the front door of the whole pipeline, because every downstream stage inherits whatever the retriever hands it, and a reranker that has to rescue a bad candidate set is spending its budget on triage rather than on the ranking work it was built to do, which is why teams that skip this step tend to discover it months later in the form of a support queue. The chunking strategy is where the bill comes due here: overlap that looks wasteful on paper is the thing that keeps a boundary from swallowing the one sentence that answered the question, and the cost of that overlap is a rounding error next to the cost of a wrong answer delivered with confidence. Embedding models are a garden that needs tending as the corpus grows, and the moment the vocabulary of new documents drifts from the vocabulary the index was built on, recall starts to bleed out quietly, which is the failure that nobody notices until a user does. Evaluation is the compass the whole effort steers by, and a suite assembled from whatever examples happened to be easy to label will point confidently in a direction nobody chose, which is how a team ends up shipping a retrieval change that scores better on the benchmark and worse for every person who actually asks the system a question.
output: Retrieval quality determines what every downstream stage receives. A reranker given a bad candidate set spends its capacity triaging candidates instead of ranking them, and teams that skip retrieval work often learn about the problem months later through support requests. Chunking is where the cost shows up: overlap may look wasteful, but it can keep a boundary from separating the sentence that answers the question, and that cost is small compared with a wrong answer delivered with confidence. Embedding models need maintenance as the corpus grows. When the vocabulary of new documents drifts from the vocabulary the index was built on, recall declines quietly, and nobody notices until a user does. Evaluation guides the work, but a suite assembled from examples that were easy to label can point confidently in a direction nobody chose. That is how a team ships a retrieval change that scores better on the benchmark and worse for every person who asks the system a question.

Chunking is where the cost shows up: overlap may look wasteful, but it can keep a boundary from separating the sentence that answers the question, and that cost is small compared with a wrong answer delivered with confidence. When the vocabulary of new documents drifts from the vocabulary the index was built on, recall declines quietly, and nobody notices until a user does. Evaluation guides the work, but a suite assembled from examples that were easy to label can point confidently in a direction nobody chose. That is how a team ships a retrieval change that scores better on the benchmark and worse for every person who asks the system a question.

input: Quantum computing has been proposed as a paradigm shift for solving certain optimization and simulation tasks. Unlike classical bits, qubits can represent superpositions, enabling parallel computation in specific problem structures. Although real-world advantage remains limited by hardware instability and error rates, research in quantum algorithms continues to expand. For industries such as logistics, chemistry, and cryptography, quantum readiness is becoming a strategic conversation. Companies can start by training technical teams and identifying quantum-friendly problem classes. Even before full-scale deployment, a quantum roadmap can act as a signal of innovation leadership and future resilience in computational competitiveness.

input: Sustainable supply chains require coordination across sourcing, production, transportation, and disposal. Academic research highlights that transparency reduces environmental and social risks, but implementation is challenging due to fragmented suppliers and inconsistent reporting standards. Technologies like blockchain and digital product passports are sometimes proposed, though their real impact depends on data accuracy and governance. For brands, sustainability claims must be evidence-based to avoid greenwashing concerns. Companies that invest in traceability can strengthen compliance readiness and customer trust. In a marketing context, transparency stories—when supported by audit data—create stronger differentiation and can justify premium pricing ethically.

input: Financial literacy is correlated with improved household resilience and long-term wealth outcomes. Studies show that individuals who understand compound interest, budgeting, and risk diversification are less likely to accumulate high-cost debt. Yet financial education initiatives often fail if they remain abstract and not connected to real behavior. Practical tools—automated savings, spending categorization, and goal-based planning—support behavioral adoption. Fintech platforms increasingly package education with product features, making learning more actionable. From a societal perspective, scaling financial capability reduces economic vulnerability. From a business angle, helping users succeed financially can increase retention and trust in financial products.

input: Peer review remains a foundational mechanism for quality control in scientific publishing, yet it is not without limitations. Critics note issues such as reviewer bias, slow turnaround times, and inconsistent standards. Nevertheless, peer review provides a filter that often improves clarity, methodology, and replicability. Emerging models include open peer review, preprint feedback systems, and post-publication evaluation. For research institutions, improving review practices can enhance credibility and accelerate innovation cycles. In an increasingly competitive academic environment, transparent and efficient peer review not only strengthens scientific integrity but also supports broader knowledge dissemination and collaboration opportunities.
